---
title: "Getting started"
---

## Installation

```bash
composer require phpstats/phibble
```

phibble requires PHP 8.3, 8.4, or 8.5, and the mbstring and PDO extensions.
These are optional:

| Optional | Enables |
| --- | --- |
| The [phit](https://github.com/phpstats/phit) extension, 0.4.0 or later | Native CSV reading in `fromCsv()`, `fromCsvChunked()`, and `csvChunks()`. Results match the PHP reader. |
| The php_polars extension from [phpolars](https://github.com/phpstats/phpolars) | `PolarsTable` and `polars()`, described in [Backends](backends.qmd). |
| `illuminate/database` | The `->toDataFrame()` and `->phibble()` macros, described in [Laravel](laravel.qmd). Laravel applications already have it. |

The examples read public datasets, such as the Palmer penguins and
nycflights13's weather, by URL from the
[PHPstats datasets](https://github.com/phpstats/datasets). Reading a URL needs
PHP's `allow_url_fopen` setting, which is on by default.

## Imports

The examples on this page use these imports:

```php
use Phibble\DataFrame;

use function Phibble\{tibble, tribble};
use function Phibble\Expr\{col, desc, mean, median, n};
```

`Phibble\Expr` has functions named `min`, `max`, `sum`, `round`, `abs`, `log`,
`floor`, `str_pad`, `str_split`, `str_replace`, and a few others that share
names with PHP built-ins. In a file that imports them, a bare `round($x)`
calls phibble's expression helper. Write `\round($x)` for PHP's function.

## Load

`DataFrame::fromCsv()` reads a CSV file, or a URL, and guesses each column's
type. Here it reads the Palmer penguins data, whose `rownames` column holds the
row numbers the table had in R. [Reading and writing data](io.qmd) covers the
options, JSON, and databases.

{{< include examples/_read-csv.md >}}

`tibble()` builds a data frame column by column:

- A list gives one value per row, and a single value is repeated.
- A closure receives the columns built so far.

These values are the first four penguins in the data:

{{< include examples/_tibble.md >}}

`tribble()` takes the column names first, then one list per row. These are the
three New York City airports from nycflights13:

{{< include examples/_tribble.md >}}

`DataFrame::fromRows()` takes a list of associative arrays, and keys missing
from a row are NA. `DataFrame::fromColumns()` takes an array of columns and
accepts explicit types.

{{< include examples/_from-rows.md >}}

## Inspect

`echo $df` prints a data frame as tibble does:

- The header gives the size, and each column shows its type.
- More than 20 rows print the first 10.
- Numbers show three significant digits.
- NA prints as `NA`, or `<NA>` in text columns.

`format(n: 30, width: 120)` prints more rows or a wider table. `glimpse()`
gives one line per column, which suits wide data frames:

{{< include examples/_glimpse.md >}}

Each column has one type from the `Phibble\Type` enum, inferred from the
values, and PHP `null` is NA in every type. [Types](types.qmd) covers
inference, casts, and factors.

Read values:

- `$df->name`, `$df['name']`, and `$df->column('name')` return a column as a
  PHP list.
- Rows are `Phibble\Row` objects, which read values as properties or array
  keys. Iterating a data frame yields its rows.
- An unknown column name throws `Phibble\Exception\ColumnNotFound`. Names are
  never matched partially.

{{< include examples/_access.md >}}

## Transform

Data frames have dplyr's functions as methods: `select()`, `filter()`,
`mutate()`, `rename()`, `arrange()`, `groupBy()`, `summarize()`, `distinct()`,
`slice()`, `head()`, and `join()`. Each returns a new data frame, and the
original never changes. [Functions and methods](reference/index.qmd) lists
them all:

{{< include examples/_immutable.md >}}

`filter()` and `mutate()` accept a row closure, which receives a `Row`.
`arrange()` takes column names, or `[name, 'desc']` pairs.

{{< include examples/_verbs.md >}}

The same methods accept [expressions](expr.qmd) built with `col()` and the
helper functions. Expressions run a whole column at a time, and SQL and Polars
tables can translate them.

{{< include examples/_verbs-expr.md >}}

PHP `null` is a missing value. Arithmetic with it gives `null`, and an
aggregate over a column that holds it gives `null` unless `na_rm: true`:

{{< include examples/_missing.md >}}

## Summarize

`groupBy()` records grouping columns, and `summarize()` (or `summarise()`)
returns one row per group:

- Groups are sorted, with NA last, as in dplyr.
- With several grouping columns, the result keeps all but the last.
- In a grouped data frame, `filter()` and `mutate()` work within each group,
  and an aggregate in `mutate()` repeats for each row of its group.
- A row closure receives the row's group as its second argument:
  `fn (Row $r, DataFrame $group) => ...`.

{{< include examples/_grouped.md >}}

Groups are the combinations that occur in the data. `groupBy($names, drop:
false)`, like dplyr's `.drop = FALSE`, also gives a factor's empty levels a
group, where `n()` and `sum()` are 0:

{{< include examples/_group-drop.md >}}

## Combine

`distinct()` keeps the first row of each combination of the given columns.
`join()` takes the other table, the keys, and the type: `inner`, `left`,
`right`, `full`, `semi`, `anti`, or `cross`. A pair such as
`['origin', 'faa']` joins keys with different names. Joins follow dplyr 1.1,
and NA keys match each other. Here each airport in nycflights13's weather data
gets its name, position, and altitude from the airports table:

{{< include examples/_join.md >}}

A condition can also compare columns, as in dplyr's `join_by()`. Here each
hour with Newark departures on 1 January 2013 gets the latest weather reading
at or before it. Newark has no reading for 17:00 UTC, so that hour takes the
16:00 reading:

{{< include examples/_join-by.md >}}

[The Table contract](contract.qmd#joins) lists the join conditions and
options.

## Output

- `toRows()` returns a list of associative arrays, and `toColumns()` an array
  of columns.
- `writeCsv($path)` and `toCsv()` write CSV as readr's `write_csv()` does.
- `toJson()` writes records, or columns with `toJson('columns')`.

[Reading and writing data](io.qmd) covers the formats.

## Method chains and the pipe operator

Methods chain on PHP 8.3, 8.4, and 8.5. On PHP 8.5, `|>` with arrow
functions runs the same pipeline. [phplyr](https://github.com/phpstats/phplyr)
provides functions that work with `|>` without arrow functions.
